newsitem.title: USA: Small consumers leery of opening U.S. power market.
newsitem.headline: Small consumers leery of opening U.S. power market.

text.p: Homeowners and the elderly Thursday warned lawmakers Thursday not to be seduced by advocates of deregulation who say electricity rates would fall for everyone if local power markets are opened to competition.

"You're banking on a theory that has never been shown to exist," Robert Johnson, executive director of the Electric Consumers Alliance, said at a Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee workshop on power market deregulation.

"Predicted price reductions are often grossly overstated," he said in testimony to the committee. "Residential and small business consumers in some areas could see price increases in a restructured environment."

Pointing to California, set to open its power markets to competition in 1998, Johnson said the fact that the state had written a 10 percent rate reduction guarantee into its deregulation law was an "implicit admission" that the free market might not necessarily lower prices for all.

John McManus, consumer committee chairman of the American Association of Retired Persons, said industrial consumers were much more likely to enjoy the benefits of being able to choose their power supplier because they have more bargaining power.

Rural consumers, concerned about losing service in a competitive market, said that they did not want to lose the ability to buy power at affordable rates from community-owned utilities willing to serve distant areas.

"Investor-owned utilities have always had a smirking disdain for the naive hick with hay in his hair and manure on his boots who thinks he can run a utility," said Carol Everman, speaking on behalf of National Grange, the oldest general U.S. farm organization.

Any federal legislation to break up utility monopolies should ensure that electricity remains accessible and affordable for everyone, allocates costs proportionally to customers' usage, and includes strong consumer protections, the groups representing the elderly and rural users said.
